metadata.title: Anaconda from Turtle | BJJ Technique | BJJ Graph
metadata.description: Learn Anaconda from Turtle in BJJ. Step-by-step execution from Turtle Top to Anaconda Control. Success: Beginner 30%, Intermediate 50%, Advanced 65%.

overview: The Anaconda from Turtle is a dynamic submission setup that transitions from turtle top position to anaconda control through a rolling motion. This technique is technically similar to the D'arce choke but requires trapping the near arm instead of the far arm, and involves rolling to your side or back rather than maintaining top position. The anaconda exploits opponent's defensive turtle posture by threading your arm under their neck while trapping their near arm, then using a figure-four grip and rolling motion to secure optimal choking angle. The execution requires precise timing - threading the arm deep with palm-down orientation, ensuring the near arm is trapped between your choking arm and their neck, locking the grip tight, and committing to the roll before opponent can defend. Your bicep compresses one carotid artery while their own trapped arm and shoulder compress the other, creating bilateral pressure. The rolling momentum is not just a finishing detail but essential for creating the proper choking angle. This technique has become a staple of modern no-gi grappling, particularly effective because the dynamic roll is unexpected and often secures the finish before opponents can defend properly.
key_principles: Thread far arm deep under neck with palm-down orientation toward near shoulder
Trap the near arm (not far arm) between your choking arm and their neck
Secure tight figure-four grip before initiating roll
Commit immediately to the roll once grip is locked - hesitation allows defense
Roll decisively to side that brings opponent over their trapped arm
Squeeze with bicep while engaging lat muscles for bilateral compression
Rolling momentum creates optimal choking angle and secures position
setup_requirements: Turtle top position established with chest pressure on opponent
Opponent's near-side arm accessible for trap
Control of opponent's near arm with your hand
Opponent has not anticipated roll or secured extremely strong base
Sufficient space to execute rolling motion
Ability to thread arm deep under neck to near shoulder

execution_steps.description: Secure turtle top with chest pressure on opponent's back while controlling their near-side arm with your hand. Maintain tight top pressure to prevent them from standing or rolling before you're ready to attack.

Thread your far-side arm under opponent's neck toward their near shoulder, maintaining palm-down position. Drive your arm deep until your wrist clears past their near shoulder to ensure proper depth for the choking position.

Ensure opponent's near arm is trapped between your choking arm and their neck - this is the critical element that distinguishes anaconda from D'arce. The near arm creates pressure on one carotid while your bicep targets the other side.

Secure figure-four grip by grabbing your own bicep with your opposite hand, eliminating all space in the lock. Grip must be extremely tight before initiating roll to prevent escape during the transition.

Roll decisively to your side or onto your back, bringing opponent with you using the momentum. Roll toward the side that brings opponent over their trapped arm for optimal pressure angle. Commit fully to the roll without hesitation.

Squeeze with your bicep while engaging lat muscles to create anaconda choke compression. Your bicep compresses one carotid artery while their trapped arm and shoulder compress the other side, creating bilateral pressure for the finish.

common_counters.counter: Pull Arm In - opponent retracts near arm before trap is secured
common_counters.your_response: Recognize early and transition to different attack from turtle top, or pursue the arm as they pull it in

common_counters.counter: Base Out - opponent posts with free arm to prevent roll
common_counters.your_response: Maintain pressure, walk your body around their base, or transition to side control position while maintaining front headlock control

common_counters.counter: Counter Roll - opponent rolls opposite direction to escape
common_counters.your_response: Maintain grip and use their momentum to adjust to new angle, or release and scramble for new position

common_counters.counter: Stand Up - explosive standing to create space before roll initiated
common_counters.your_response: Follow them up maintaining front headlock position, or adjust to standing anaconda setup

common_errors.error: Trapping far arm instead of near arm
common_errors.consequence: Changes technique to D'arce instead of anaconda, requires different finishing angle and mechanics, cannot generate effective pressure even with correct roll
common_errors.correction: Identify which arm is closest to you (near arm) and trap that one specifically for anaconda mechanics. Near arm trap is what defines the anaconda.

common_errors.error: Hesitating or delaying the roll after securing grip
common_errors.consequence: Gives opponent time to base out with free arm and prevent roll completion, losing the momentum advantage
common_errors.correction: Commit immediately to roll once figure-four grip is locked tight. Speed and decisiveness are critical - the roll must happen before they can react.

common_errors.error: Rolling in wrong direction or insufficient roll momentum
common_errors.consequence: Incorrect angle prevents proper carotid compression, technique feels weak despite having proper arm trap and grip
common_errors.correction: Roll decisively to the side that brings opponent over their trapped arm. Commit fully to the rolling motion with momentum.

common_errors.error: Not maintaining tight grip during roll transition
common_errors.consequence: Loose grip allows opponent to create space and escape during the rolling motion when position is most vulnerable
common_errors.correction: Lock figure-four grip extremely tight before initiating roll. Maintain maximum tightness throughout entire rolling transition.

common_errors.error: Threading arm too shallow, not reaching past near shoulder
common_errors.consequence: Insufficient arm depth means proper choking position is never achieved, cannot secure effective squeeze even after rolling
common_errors.correction: Drive threading arm deep until wrist clearly clears opponent's near shoulder. Depth is essential for proper mechanics.

training_progressions.focus: Rolling motion and arm threading mechanics
training_progressions.description: Practice rolling motion with grappling dummy to develop coordination. Work arm threading depth and palm-down positioning without resistance.
Partner allows trap and roll so you can develop smooth timing between grip lock and roll initiation. Focus on feeling proper depth and tight grip before rolling.
Partner actively defends with base-out attempts and counter-roll defense. Learn to commit to roll decisively and adjust to defensive reactions.
Identify near-arm trap opportunities when opponent turtles during live rolling. Develop ability to recognize setup windows and commit to technique.
Work with advanced partners who defend with various reactions. Learn to adjust roll direction, maintain control during scrambles, and finish from different angles.

variants_and_adaptations.description: Can use gi grips for additional control though technique is primarily designed for no-gi. Collar grips can supplement the figure-four.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: In gi training when additional grip options are available

variants_and_adaptations.description: Primary application relying entirely on arm trap and body mechanics. Pure figure-four grip without gi assists.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: No-gi competition, submission grappling, MMA applications

variants_and_adaptations.description: If opponent stands up during setup, follow them up and finish anaconda from standing front headlock position.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: When opponent attempts to escape by standing before roll is initiated

variants_and_adaptations.description: More aggressive rolling motion with multiple rotations to disorient opponent and secure finish.
variants_and_adaptations.when_to_use: Against extremely defensive opponents or to increase finishing momentum

knowledge_assessment.question: What creates the choking pressure in the anaconda from turtle?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The choking pressure comes from bilateral compression - your bicep squeezes one carotid artery while the opponent's own trapped near arm and shoulder compress the other carotid. This dual-sided pressure is what makes the anaconda effective, distinguishing it from single-sided chokes.

knowledge_assessment.question: When should you initiate the roll in the anaconda setup?
knowledge_assessment.answer: You should initiate the roll immediately after locking the figure-four grip while opponent is still adjusting. Hesitation gives them time to base out and prevent the roll. Speed and commitment are critical - the roll must happen before they can react defensively.

knowledge_assessment.question: Which arm should be trapped for the anaconda from turtle?
knowledge_assessment.answer: The near arm (closest to you) must be trapped for the anaconda. This is what distinguishes anaconda from D'arce choke, which traps the far arm. The near arm trap is essential for creating proper pressure angle after the roll.

knowledge_assessment.question: What must be accomplished before rolling in the anaconda setup?
knowledge_assessment.answer: Before rolling you must achieve: (1) near arm trapped between your choking arm and their neck, (2) deep arm threading with wrist past near shoulder, and (3) tight figure-four grip secured. All three elements must be in place or the roll will fail.

knowledge_assessment.question: How do you adjust if opponent bases out during your roll attempt?
knowledge_assessment.answer: If opponent bases out, maintain pressure and grip, then walk your body around their posted base to find a new rolling angle. Alternatively, transition to side control while maintaining front headlock control, or attack different submission from the modified position.

safety_considerations: When practicing the anaconda from turtle, execute the rolling motion smoothly and controlled to prevent partner from landing awkwardly or being thrown. Apply choking pressure gradually in training, never explosively. Monitor partner's response carefully and release immediately upon tap signal. Ensure partner is prepared for the rolling motion before initiating. Be particularly mindful of neck safety during the roll transition. In drilling, use progressive resistance to build coordination before attempting at full speed. Partners should communicate clearly about comfort level with rolling techniques.
position_integration: The anaconda from turtle is part of the front headlock family and represents a high-level submission setup from turtle top control. It connects to the broader turtle attack system where you have options including back takes, guillotines, D'arce chokes, and now the anaconda. The technique is particularly valuable because turtle is a common defensive position in both gi and no-gi grappling. When opponents turtle to defend guard passes or back attacks, the anaconda becomes available. It integrates with modern no-gi systems emphasizing front headlock control, submission wrestling, and dynamic transitions. The rolling element makes it especially effective in scramble situations where momentum can be used to your advantage. In competition, it serves as both a submission threat and position improvement tool - even if the choke doesn't finish, you often establish dominant side control or back position. The anaconda has become fundamental in 10th Planet Jiu-Jitsu and Eddie Bravo's system, as well as in submission grappling competitions like ADCC where turtle attacks are heavily rewarded.

expert_insights.danaher: The anaconda from turtle is technically similar to the D'arce but requires an additional element of rolling to secure the optimal finishing angle. The critical distinction is that you trap the near arm rather than the far arm, and the finish typically involves rolling to your side or back rather than staying on top. Thread your arm deep with palm down, ensuring the near arm is trapped. The rolling motion is not just a finishing detail - it's essential for creating the proper choking angle. Your bicep must compress one side while their own trapped arm and shoulder compress the other carotid artery.
expert_insights.gordon_ryan: The anaconda from turtle is one of my favorite techniques because it's unexpected and the roll momentum often secures the finish before they can defend properly. The key is committing to the roll once you have the grip - hesitation gives them time to base out. I thread the arm, lock the grip, and immediately roll to my side. Even if the choke doesn't finish right away, I've usually secured top position with a dominant control. It's a high-reward technique when executed with speed and confidence.
expert_insights.eddie_bravo: We use the anaconda constantly in our system, especially from turtle and during scrambles. The beautiful thing about the anaconda is the roll - it's dynamic, it's aggressive, and opponents don't see it coming. Once you get comfortable with that gator roll motion, you can hit anacondas from all kinds of positions. From turtle it's especially good because they're already in a compromised position. Thread deep, trap that near arm, and roll hard. The momentum does half the work for you.
